---
title: "QK routing: a failed attempt at MoE-inspired sparse attention"
---

Over about eight months this line of work tried to make attention sparse the way
Mixture-of-Experts made the feed-forward network sparse: instead of every query
attending densely to the whole KV cache, route each query to a small set of
learned **partitions** of the cache and attend only there. If it worked, the
payoff would be a smaller KV-cache read at inference — the dominant
memory-and-latency cost of long-context serving — bought without hurting
language-modeling quality.

It did not work. Across **230 runs on five datasets** — 136 in the "clustering"
lineage, 75 in the "partition" lineage, and 19 dense baselines — no
configuration beat, and only a handful matched, the dense ALiBi baseline it
started from. This report compiles the whole arc: where the idea came from, how
it mutated from hard k-means clustering into soft learned routing into a
MoE-style partition gate, exactly why each incarnation failed, and — because the
failures turned out to be well-understood ones that the field has since
solved — what a corrected attempt (and the custom kernels it would need) should
look like.

::: {.callout-note}
## The one-sentence version
Training loss was never the problem — every variant trained down to roughly the
dense baseline. The problem was always the *sparse* attention path: it never
received a language-modeling gradient, it was graded at eval on a routing it was
never trained through, and its objective rewarded collapse. The most honest
commit in the entire history reads: *"sparse clustering... recalls 40% with 40%
of keys."* That is the ceiling, stated plainly.
:::

## Where the idea came from

The lineage literally grew out of an MLA experiment (`ce43340 "setup mla"`). The
motivating analogy: MoE routes each token to $k$ of $N$ expert FFNs and only pays
for those $k$; attention, by contrast, pays for the *entire* KV cache on every
query. If a query could be routed to a few relevant partitions of the cache —
"these 2 of 64 partitions hold what this query needs" — the inference-time KV
read would shrink by the sparsity factor. That is the thesis the whole project
was testing.

Two design choices, made early, shaped everything downstream:

- **Routing on the positionless projection.** Queries and keys were routed using
  their *content* projection with no position encoding (`ln_q_nope`,
  `ln_k_nope`, `apply_rope=False`), while **ALiBi** carried position separately.
  This is structurally the same content/position split that DeepSeek's MLA makes
  with its *decoupled RoPE* — the routing decision is content-based, position is
  bolted on. The project was decoupling position from routing from day one; it
  just used ALiBi's recency bias to do it (a choice that, in hindsight, actively
  fought the retrieval objective — see [Why it failed](#why-it-failed)).
- **Hard routing is the deployment behavior.** At inference each query must
  attend within its routed partition(s) only — that is where the KV saving comes
  from — so evaluation *correctly* forces the hard mask (via `total_steps=0`, so
  every schedule threshold is met at step 0). The failure is never that eval is
  "unfair"; it is that training rarely matched what eval graded.

## Two lineages, one dead end

What looks like a single chain of branches is really **two independent trees**
that converge on the same design and the same wall.

| Era | Branch | Idea | Dataset(s) | Runs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Tree A** — hard clustering | `cluster_qk` | k-means attention: argmax-assign each q and k to a cluster, attend iff same cluster | slim, starcoder | 30 |
| | `cluster_qk_alibi` | same, on the ALiBi baseline | slim | 31 |
| | `cluster_qk_alibi_v2` | split q/k centroids; attention-aware key objective; skip layer 0 | slim | 8 |
| **Tree B** — soft routing | `cluster_qk_alibi_lora` | **fresh start off `alibi`**: soft `sigmoid` query gate + `softmax` key router, outer-product keep-mask, soft→hard schedule, recall/retrieve budget loss | slim | 66 |
| | `cluster_qk_alibi_lora_mlp_q` | nonlinear (SwiGLU) query gate | slim | 1 |
| **Partition** — Tree B, renamed + extended | `parition_qk_alibi` | Tree B's routing, `clusters`→`partitions` | c4, slim | 1 |
| | `..._embed` | route off the layer-input embedding $g_x$, not q/k | c4, slim | 23 |
| | `..._embed_mlp_q` | MLP query gate | — | — |
| | `..._embed_post_training` | freeze a pretrained dense model, tune only routing | c4, longcrawl | 32 |
| | `..._embed_post_training_no_stats` | logging only | — | — |
| | `..._embed_post_training_retrieval_penalty` | add a sparsity-budget loss term | c4 | 19 |

Two facts this table encodes that the branch names hide:

1. **The partition lineage is not descended from the clustering lineage.** The
   soft-routing branch `cluster_qk_alibi_lora` was branched *fresh off the dense
   `alibi` baseline*, not off the hard-clustering code (`git merge-base` confirms
   it shares only the old pre-clustering ancestor). `parition_qk_alibi` is then
   essentially `cluster_qk_alibi_lora` with three renames
   (`clusters`→`partitions`, `q_clusters`→`w_q_gate`, `k_clusters`→`w_k_routing`)
   plus two additions (route off $g_x$; add post-training). **The conceptual
   jump — hard argmax clustering to soft learned routing — happened *inside* the
   clustering lineage, not between the two.**
2. **The two lineages never shared a comparison dataset except slim.** Clustering
   ran only on slim and starcoder; partition ran only on c4, slim, and
   longcrawl. **Slim is the only apples-to-apples ground** between them — and on
   slim, both top out at the *same* number (eval ≈ 1.85, ppl ≈ 6.3), i.e. dense
   parity, via completely different machinery.

## The mechanism, and how it mutated

Every variant is a specialization of one skeleton. Per attention layer, on top
of standard ALiBi-causal attention with scores `logits` and
`probs = softmax(logits)`:

1. **Route the query and the key.** Produce, per partition, a query "gate" and a
   key "assignment":
   $$
   \texttt{q\_gate} = \sigma(g \cdot W_q) \in [0,1]^{N},\qquad
   \texttt{k\_route} = \mathrm{softmax}(g \cdot W_k) \in \Delta^{N}
   $$
   where $g$ is the routing input ($\mathrm{norm}(q)$/$\mathrm{norm}(k)$ early,
   the layer-input embedding $g_x$ in the `_embed` variants) and $N$ is the
   partition count.
2. **Form a keep-mask.** The outer product over partitions gives a soft
   keep-probability per (query, key) pair,
   `softmask = einsum(q_gate, k_route) * causal`.
3. **Attend through the mask.** Either `probs * softmask` (early branches) or a
   re-softmax with `log(softmask)` as an additive bias (later branches).
4. **Train the router by an auxiliary loss** (`recall_loss`, `retrieve_loss`) —
   *not* directly by the LM loss.
5. **Schedule soft→hard.** `apply_softmask` and `apply_hardmask` switch on at
   `step >= start_fraction * total_steps`. The **hard** path
   (`q_gate > threshold`, $\arg\max$ over `k_route`) is the inference behavior;
   eval forces it with `total_steps=0`.

The mutation across the arc is entirely in *how q and k get routed* and *how the
router is trained*:

| | Routing unit | Query side | Key side | Router trained by | Train/eval |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `cluster_qk` / `_alibi` | cluster (hard) | $\arg\max(nq\cdot C)$ | $\arg\max(nk\cdot C)$, shared centroids $C$ | k-means alignment loss | on from step 0 |
| `cluster_qk_alibi_v2` | cluster (hard) | $\arg\max(nq\cdot C_q)$ | key-centroid picked by q's cluster, aligned to prob-weighted attended key | attention-aware k-means | on from step 0 |
| `cluster_qk_alibi_lora` | cluster (soft) | $\sigma(nq\cdot C_q)$ | $\mathrm{softmax}(nk\cdot C_k)$ | recall − retrieve budget | soft/hard start-fractions |
| `parition_qk_alibi(_embed)` | partition (soft) | $\sigma(g\cdot W_q)$ | $\mathrm{softmax}(g\cdot W_k)$ | recall − retrieve budget | soft/hard start-fractions |

The through-line: **from a symmetric geometric clustering trained by a k-means
objective that is structurally decoupled from the LM loss → to an asymmetric
learned gate/router trained by a recall/sparsity budget that is *still*
decoupled from the LM loss.** That decoupling — the router never being told, by
the thing that actually matters, that its routing was bad — is the single thread
that runs unbroken through all 211 routing runs.

```{python}
# | code-fold: true
# | code-summary: "Data-loading harness (shared by all figures)"
import csv
import json
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.io as pio

pio.renderers.default = "plotly_mimetype+notebook_connected"
ROOT = Path("../clearml_experiments")
PALETTE = ["#1f77b4", "#ff7f0e", "#2ca02c", "#d62728", "#9467bd",
           "#8c564b", "#e377c2", "#7f7f7f", "#bcbd22", "#17becf"]


def ema(xs, s=0.97):
    out = [xs[0]]
    for v in xs[1:]:
        out.append(out[-1] * s + v * (1 - s))
    return out


def read_csv(p):
    if not p.exists():
        return None
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(open(p)))
    if not rows:
        return None
    return [int(float(r["step"])) for r in rows], [float(r["value"]) for r in rows]


def load_run(d):
    md = json.loads((d / "metadata.json").read_text())
    m = d / "metrics"
    train = read_csv(m / "loss_loss.csv")
    ev = read_csv(m / "final_loss_eval.csv")
    cfg = {k.split(".", 1)[1]: v for k, v in md.get("hyperparameters", {}).items()
           if k.startswith("Hydra/model.") or k.startswith("Hydra/training.")}
    return {
        "name": md["experiment_name"], "status": md["status"], "config": cfg,
        "train_steps": train[0] if train else None,
        "train_loss": train[1] if train else None,
        "train_ema": ema(train[1])[-1] if train else None,
        "eval": ev[1][-1] if ev else None,
        "n_clusters": int(cfg.get("n_clusters", cfg.get("n_partitions", 0)) or 0),
    }


def load_group(rel):
    p = ROOT / rel
    if not p.exists():
        return []
    return [load_run(d) for d in sorted(p.iterdir()) if d.is_dir()
            and (d / "metadata.json").exists()]
```

## What the numbers show

### Training always looked healthy

The first and most misleading signal: **train loss was never the problem.**
Every stage of the clustering lineage — hard clustering, split-centroid v2, soft
LoRA routing — trains down to essentially the dense slim baseline (train ≈ 1.78).
The routing masks are either off during training (the default schedule) or, when
on, contribute no useful gradient, so the model is effectively training as dense
ALiBi and the curve looks fine. Nothing here warns you that eval will collapse.

```{python}
# | code-fold: true
# | code-summary: "Clustering lineage: best train curve per stage (slim)"
STAGES = [
    ("cluster_qk", "slim_v4_32_31m/cluster_qk", "#1f77b4"),
    ("cluster_qk_alibi", "slim_v4_32_31m/cluster_qk_alibi", "#ff7f0e"),
    ("cluster_qk_alibi_v2", "slim_v4_32_31m/cluster_qk_alibi_v2", "#2ca02c"),
    ("cluster_qk_alibi_lora", "slim_v4_32_31m/cluster_qk_alibi_lora", "#9467bd"),
]
fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_hline(y=1.78, line=dict(color="black", dash="dash"),
              annotation_text="dense ALiBi (slim train ≈ 1.78)",
              annotation_position="top right")
for label, rel, color in STAGES:
    runs = [r for r in load_group(rel) if r["train_loss"] is not None
            and r["train_ema"] is not None and r["train_ema"] > 1.0]  # drop 0.0 crashes
    if not runs:
        continue
    best = min(runs, key=lambda r: r["train_ema"])
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=best["train_steps"], y=ema(best["train_loss"]),
                             mode="lines", name=label, line=dict(color=color, width=2),
                             hovertemplate="%{fullData.name}<br>step=%{x}<br>loss=%{y:.3f}<extra></extra>"))
fig.update_layout(xaxis_title="Step", yaxis_title="Training loss (EMA)", height=460,
                  yaxis_range=[1.6, 3.0],
                  legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="top", y=-0.2, xanchor="center", x=0.5),
                  margin=dict(l=60, r=20, t=20, b=80))
fig.show()
```

Most clustering runs logged train loss *only* — no eval — which is itself part
of the story: the lineage was steered by the curve that looked good, and the
eval-time collapse (where it was measured at all) was under-instrumented until
late. Cross-group eval comparison exists cleanly only for the partition-embed
groups and the one LoRA group with eval logged.

### Eval never beat dense — both lineages plateau at parity

On slim, the *only* dataset the two lineages share, they land on the same number
from opposite directions:

```{python}
# | code-fold: true
# | code-summary: "Slim: best eval per lineage vs dense"
rows = [
    {"lineage": "dense ALiBi", "config": "baseline", "eval": None, "ppl": None,
     "train": 1.78, "note": "baseline (eval not logged; train 1.78)"},
    {"lineage": "cluster (soft/lora)", "config": "n_clusters=512", "eval": 1.849, "ppl": 6.36,
     "train": None, "note": "best of 66 LoRA runs"},
    {"lineage": "partition (embed)", "config": "n_part=512", "eval": 1.848, "ppl": 6.35,
     "train": 1.78, "note": "best of 15 partition-embed runs"},
    {"lineage": "partition (embed)", "config": "plain routed, 512-part", "eval": 4.58, "ppl": 97.0,
     "train": None, "note": "worst — routing engaged, collapsed"},
]
pd.DataFrame(rows).style.format({"eval": "{:.3f}", "ppl": "{:.1f}", "train": "{:.2f}"},
                                na_rep="—").hide(axis="index").set_caption(
    "slim: both lineages top out at dense parity (~1.85 / ppl 6.3); neither improves on it.")
```

On c4 and longcrawl — where only the partition lineage ran — it is strictly
worse: c4 active-partition runs land at eval 3.55–3.74 (ppl 34.7–42.2) versus
dense 3.49 (32.6); the best longcrawl post-training result reaches 3.37 versus
dense 3.17, **+0.2 nats**. Every partition figure that isn't an artifact of the
routing failing to engage is above the dense baseline.

### The train/eval gap is a schedule artifact — and closing it reveals the real ceiling

The most violent numbers (c4 eval 6.2; slim 512-partition eval 4.58) are a
**train/eval mismatch**, not an inherent property of hard routing. With the
default `softmask_start_fraction = hardmask_start_fraction = 1.0`, the masks
never activate during training — the model trains dense and meets its own hard
routing for the first time at eval. Runs that reach the hard mask *during*
training (`hard_frac < 1.0`) close the gap to ≈ 0, exactly as they should, since
train and eval then use the same routing. The mismatch is removable. What
remains once it is closed is the method's real ceiling: matched-schedule and
post-training runs are train/eval-consistent but still land **~0.1–0.4 nats
above dense**, because the routing objective and masked-attention math cannot
learn a sparse pattern that preserves quality. The partition report
([`partition_qk_alibi.qmd`](partition_qk_alibi.qmd)) works this schedule story
through run by run.

### Post-training loss only ever rose; the retrieval penalty optimized the wrong thing

Two clean demonstrations of the objective being broken rather than the
optimization being unlucky:

- **Post-training** (freeze a dense model, tune only the routing) is the purest
  test — no train/eval mismatch, since it trains through the soft-into-hard
  schedule. On longcrawl every run's CE rises *monotonically from its step-0
  minimum* (the dense starting point). Freezing the language model and letting
  only the router move cannot recover the quality the partition mask removes.
- **The retrieval-penalty branch** adds `retrieve_loss = mean_layers log(retrieved_fraction)`,
  a *negative* quantity *added* to the loss — so total loss drops when fewer keys
  are retrieved, regardless of CE. The trap is visible directly: total loss falls
  below zero while CE climbs to ≈ 9.5 (eval perplexity **12k–13k**, near random
  init). The optimizer is cashing in language-modeling quality for the sparsity
  reward.

## Why it failed {#why-it-failed}

The line-level bugs (below) are real and each maps to a measured failure, but the
method would not have worked even bug-free, for four structural reasons:

1. **The router never received a language-modeling gradient.** This is the
   unbroken thread. In Tree A the mask is a non-differentiable $\arg\max$ and the
   alignment is `stop_gradient`'d, so CE contributes *zero* gradient to the
   clustering — routing quality is decoupled from LM quality by construction. In
   Tree B the soft path in the *base* and `_mlp_q` branches is literally
   `stop_gradient(probs) * softmask`. (Nuance the earlier partition writeup got
   wrong: the `_embed`/`_post_training`/`_no_stats`/`_retrieval_penalty` branches
   *did* fix this — they re-softmax with `log(softmask)` as an additive bias, so
   CE does reach the routing weights. But in the default schedule the soft mask
   is off during training anyway, so on those branches the router still learned
   from CE only if a schedule override turned masking on.) Either way, the router
   was overwhelmingly trained by a proxy objective, not by the loss it needed to
   minimize.
2. **The router was graded on a routing it was never trained through.** Hard
   routing is the correct eval, but the default schedule trained dense. Train ≠
   test, catastrophically and seed-dependently.
3. **The routing objective rewarded collapse.** `recall_loss` (and its ratio and
   budget variants) has no load-balancing or entropy term. Routing every key to
   one partition and opening that gate maximizes recall — a valid minimizer that
   destroys the whole point. The retrieval penalty made this worse by adding a
   sparsity reward that trades directly against CE.
4. **ALiBi's recency prior fought the retrieval thesis.** ALiBi is a hard-coded
   linear distance penalty — it hands the model locality for free. But the entire
   value proposition of routing is attending to a *distant, relevant* partition.
   The router had to overcome a built-in local bias just to justify any
   long-range retrieval. A distance-neutral encoding (RoPE, or NoPE + a decoupled
   RoPE sub-vector) is a far better substrate for *learned* sparsity — and the
   routing was already running on the positionless projection, so the position
   encoding was a free variable that happened to be set adversarially.

### Consolidated code defects

Verified against the branch code. Line refs are on the `old_experiments` remote.

| # | Defect | Where | Failure signature |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Router never trained.** `*_start_fraction` defaults to `1.0`; no from-scratch config overrides it, so masks are off in training. Model trains dense, meets hard routing only at eval. (Fix is on the *training* side: keep hard eval, set `hard_frac < 1.0`.) | Hparams default; `base:101–102`, gate `609–610` | eval blows up & seed-dependent **only at** `hard_frac=1.0`; matched schedules → gap ≈ 0 |
| 2 | **Masked probs not renormalized.** Hard path does `probs * hardmask` with no re-softmax, shrinking output by the recall fraction. Scoped to `base` + `_mlp_q` (other branches re-softmax). | `base:653`, `mlpq:732` | the c4 `base` run eval 6.2 (renormalizing branches don't show this) |
| 3 | **Objective rewards collapse.** `recall_loss` has no load-balance/entropy; `retrieve_loss` is negative-and-added. | all; penalty in `_retrieval_penalty` (`rp:793–802`) | total loss ↓ (even < 0) while CE ↑ |
| 4 | **`stop_gradient` on the attention distribution** kills CE→router gradient — but **only in `base` + `_mlp_q`** (`stop_gradient(probs)*softmask`). The `_embed`/`_post_training`/`_no_stats`/`_retrieval_penalty` branches re-softmax and *do* pass CE gradient to the routing weights. | `base:611`, `mlpq:688` | mask-on training degrades CE monotonically (base/mlpq only) |
| 5 | **Gate bias dead or hardcoded.** `q_bias` never added before `sigmoid` in `base`/`_embed`; hardcoded `+20.0` in `_retrieval_penalty` (`rp:434`), saturating the gate open and making the `_w_bias_10/_100` "sweep" a no-op. | `base:433/596`, `rp:434/599` | gate ≈ 1.0; "sweep" runs identical |
| 6 | **Mis-horizoned post-training LR.** Post phase shrinks `steps`/`warmup` but not `steps_for_lr`, so cosine traverses ~⅓ of its arc and LR stays near-peak; then ×`post_training_mult` (0.125–5.0). | `pt:1277–1286`, `pt:1042–1046` | routing never converges; loss rises from step 0 |
| 7 | **Stale grad-norm exclusion.** Clip filter skips `q_clusters`/`k_clusters` (names that no longer exist after the rename); the real weights `w_q_gate`/`w_k_routing` fall through and get clipped, pinning the logged `grad_norm` at 1.00 and hiding #6. `raw_grad_norm` had the true value. | `base:1030–1034` | grad-norm pinned at 1.00 everywhere |

Tree A carried its own earlier versions of the same pathologies: a
`-1e10`-everywhere softmax row that silently returns **uniform weights over
future keys** (a causal leak) when a query's cluster matches no causal key
(`cluster_qk_alibi:547`); centroids excluded from the clip norm but updated at LR
1.0, with the author's own commit noting *"grad norms still exploding :("*; and
random routing applied from step 0 (`clustering_start_fraction=0.0`) corrupting
the most fragile phase of training.

## What the field did that worked

Every structural failure above has since been fixed — separately — in three
published designs. Read the other way, they are a checklist of what this project
got wrong:

| What broke here | The fix, and who shipped it |
|---|---|
| Router trained by a proxy, not by CE (#1, #3, #4) | **NSA** (DeepSeek, [2502.11089](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.11089)) is *"natively trainable... unlike baselines which train with full attention and apply sparsity post-hoc."* Sparsity is in the forward path from step 0 and the selection is differentiable end-to-end. |
| Ad-hoc gate/router, no MoE-style balancing (#3) | **MoBA** (Moonshot/Kimi, [2502.13189](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13189)) — literally "Mixture of Block Attention": MoE gating routes each query to a subset of KV *blocks*, with a seamless full↔sparse switch. This is the design this project was groping toward. |
| Router got no LM-quality signal (#4) | **DSA** (DeepSeek-V3.2, [2512.02556](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02556)) trains a lightweight **lightning indexer** (multi-head ReLU-gated scores) to pick top-k=2048 tokens. Its successor makes the indexer **natively trainable end-to-end** — no collapse-prone budget loss at all. |
| Masking added compute instead of saving it | All are paired with **hardware-aligned kernels** (blockwise selection to keep memory access contiguous). Sparsity you can't turn into a faster kernel is just overhead — see below. |

### DeepSeek-V4 fuses all three of these threads — and does the RoPE trick this project's author independently proposed

**DeepSeek-V4** (open-weight MoE, released Apr 24 2026;
[2606.19348](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19348)) is the culmination, and it is
worth dwelling on because it is essentially *every* idea in this report, done
right and fused into one architecture. It interleaves two attention types:

- **Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA)** — compress every $m$ tokens into one KV
  entry, then apply DSA **top-k selection over the compressed entries** via a
  **low-rank "lightning indexer"** that is *natively trainable end-to-end* (no
  auxiliary or distillation loss for the router). Block-level, `c4a` ≈ 4×
  compression, $k=512$. **This is the corrected version of qk-routing**:
  block-level, natively trainable, an indexer instead of a collapse-rewarding
  recall budget, sparsity in the forward path from step 0.
- **Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA)** — much more aggressive temporal
  compression (`c128a` ≈ 128×) but **dense** attention over the few remaining
  compressed tokens. **This is the LCM / KV-compression direction**
  ([`lcm.qmd`](lcm.qmd)).

The payoff: at 1M-token context, V4-Pro uses **27% of the single-token inference
FLOPs and 10% of the KV cache** of V3.2, on fused kernels (compressor +
RMSNorm + RoPE; inverse-RoPE + fp8; an FP4 indexer).

**The RoPE detail is the one to notice.** V4 *shares* its K and V vectors and
compresses them — and with a shared vector you cannot RoPE it for the key role
without also rotating it in the value role. V4's answer is exactly the
"rope-then-un-rope-the-output" operation: it applies RoPE to the last 64
(decoupled) dimensions of the shared/compressed KV entry at its absolute
position $j$, and after attention applies **RoPE with position $-i$** (the query
position) to the *output*. The value path $\sum_j a_{ij} R_j v_j$ becomes
$R_{-i}\sum_j a_{ij} R_j v_j = \sum_j a_{ij} R_{j-i} v_j$ — every value rotated by
its **relative** offset to the query, restoring translation invariance under
shared KV. It is the enabling trick for shared-KV + RoPE, and it composes
directly with the **shared-KV work already in this repo**
([`shared_kv.qmd`](shared_kv.qmd)): shared-KV made RoPE incompatible, and this
is the fix.

## Future directions

### 1. Fix the method

A corrected experiment would combine, for the first time, every fix — no run
ever did:

| Fix | Defect addressed |
|---|---|
| Train through the hard mask (keep hard eval; set `hard_frac < 1.0`, or use a straight-through estimator) so training sees the routing it is graded on | #1 |
| Re-softmax (renormalize) attention after masking, on every branch | #2 |
| Add a load-balancing / entropy term; delete the sign-flipped budget reward. Or drop the hand-built objective entirely and **distill the dense attention distribution** into the router (the DSA move) | #3 |
| Let CE flow into the router everywhere (no `stop_gradient` on `probs`) | #4 |
| Make the gate bias an annealed hparam, not a hardcoded constant | #5 |
| Fix the post-training LR horizon (`steps_for_lr = steps // 3`) | #6 |
| Fix the grad-norm exclusion to the real weight names | #7 |
| **Swap ALiBi for RoPE or NoPE + decoupled-RoPE** so the position encoding stops fighting long-range retrieval. `position_embeddings.qmd` already has the dense RoPE-vs-ALiBi comparison at this scale to seed the choice; if combined with shared-KV, use V4's RoPE / inverse-RoPE-on-the-output trick (see above) | structural #4 |

Prefer **block-level** routing (MoBA/NSA/V4-CSA) over the per-key partition mask:
selecting contiguous KV blocks is both easier to load-balance and the only kind
of sparsity a TPU/GPU kernel can actually exploit.

### 2. Or change the mechanism, not just fix it

The *goal* was shrinking the KV cache. Sparse routing is one way; **low-rank KV
compression (MLA)** is the proven other way, and there is already an `mla` branch
in the repo. MLA gets the same inference-time saving without a router to train,
sidestepping the entire failure mode documented here. Given that this lineage
literally began as an MLA experiment, closing the loop back to MLA is the most
direct path to the original objective.

But the sharper target is **DeepSeek-V4's synthesis**, because it unifies three
things this repo already has separate branches for: shared-KV
([`shared_kv.qmd`](shared_kv.qmd)), KV compression
([`lcm.qmd`](lcm.qmd)), and the sparse routing documented here. V4's recipe —
**HCA** (heavy temporal compression + dense attention, i.e. the LCM idea) on most
layers, **CSA** (light compression + natively-trainable top-k block selection,
i.e. the *fixed* qk-routing) on the rest, shared-KV with the RoPE/inverse-RoPE
trick throughout — is a concrete, published blueprint for combining all three
into one model rather than testing them in isolation.

### 3. Custom kernels — the actually-important lesson

The quiet reason this project was slow to iterate: **the routing never made
training faster — it made it slower.** Masking `probs` with a `softmask` and
adding recall/retrieve losses *adds* FLOPs and materializes extra `[L, L]`-shaped
tensors on top of dense attention. The sparsity existed only in the *math*, never
in the *kernel*, so there was no compute or memory payoff to offset the quality
loss — the experiment paid the sparsity tax without collecting the sparsity
refund. Any serious retry has to make the sparse path a *real* sparse kernel:

- **On TPU (where seqax runs), the tool is Pallas + SplashAttention.** JAX ships
  a TPU-native, sparse-aware Flash Attention
  ([`splash_attention_kernel.py`](https://github.com/jax-ml/jax/blob/main/jax/experimental/pallas/ops/tpu/splash_attention/splash_attention_kernel.py))
  that takes a **block-sparse mask** and skips the masked blocks entirely — it is
  the default attention kernel in MaxText. A MoBA/NSA-style *block* router maps
  directly onto it: the router picks blocks, SplashAttention computes only the
  chosen blocks, and both the compute *and* the KV read shrink by the sparsity
  factor. This is the missing piece — the reason to make the routing block-level
  rather than per-key.
- **Token-level selection (DSA) needs a gather kernel**, not just a masked one:
  after top-k the selected KV entries are scattered in memory, so the kernel must
  gather them into a dense tile before the MXU/Tensor-Core matmul. That is a
  harder kernel to write (Pallas on TPU, Triton on GPU) but it is what makes
  finer-grained sparsity pay off, and it is exactly what V3.2 built.
- **Consequence for the design:** the kernel constraint should *drive* the
  routing granularity, not the other way around. Per-(query,key) partition masks
  — what this project built — are the least kernel-friendly choice possible.
  Blockwise selection (contiguous, MXU-tile-aligned) is what both makes the
  method trainable-at-speed and gives the KV-cache saving that motivated the
  whole thing.

The honest summary is that this was the right problem approached with the wrong
three choices — a non-differentiable/proxy-trained router, a collapse-rewarding
objective, and math-only sparsity with no kernel — each of which the field has
since shown how to make. A retry that trains the router through the mask,
distills the dense distribution into it, routes at block granularity, and runs on
SplashAttention would be testing a genuinely different hypothesis than any of
these 230 runs did.

## Limitations

- All runs are ~31M parameters (c4/slim at $L=1024$, longcrawl long-context). The
  mechanism could behave differently at scale.
- Eval coverage is uneven: most clustering runs and several baselines logged
  train loss only, so some cross-group comparisons rest on train loss plus the
  runs where eval exists.
- Many runs marked `failed` in ClearML actually finished training and eval — the
  crash is a checkpoint-upload/teardown error after metrics were logged; those
  eval numbers are valid. A minority are genuine collapses (ppl 12k+, duplicated
  eval rows) and are filtered out of the figures.
- No run combined the corrected design (train-through-hard-mask + renormalized
  attention + load-balanced/distilled objective + a real sparse kernel). The
  fixed method was never tested.
- Results are loss-only. No KV-cache memory or inference latency was ever
  measured — so even the runs that reached dense parity never demonstrated the
  saving that was the entire point.
